corrections.caveats: Independent third-party suite (scikit-learn project's ml-benchmarks by Fabian Pedregosa, code public in benchmarks/), but from July 2011 with Shogun 0.10.0 and scikit-learn 0.8, both far out of date; scikit-learn's KMeans has since been rewritten, so the result says nothing about current versions. Compiler, flags and BLAS build are not stated, so B and not A. Timings go through the Python interfaces, so interface overhead is included. The page itself says 'Note: The shogun is failling ..' next to the k-means section and leaves the Shogun inertia for Arcene blank, so the Arcene win (0.19 s vs 0.51 s) is unconfirmed; Madelon inertia 7.3x10^8 (Shogun) vs 7.4x10^8 (scikit-learn) matches. Settings are not equalised: the harness passes n_init=1 to scikit-learn and runs Shogun's KMeans with its defaults. The bench_kmeans.py at HEAD imports 'sklearn' (the post-0.9 package name) while its inertia helper imports 'scikits.learn', so the public code is a later revision than the one that produced the July 2011 table. Shogun is not the fastest on Madelon k-means (milk 0.67 s) and is slower than scikit-learn on SVM (Madelon 5.63 s vs 5.20 s, Arcene 0.39 s vs 0.38 s) and nearest neighbours (Madelon 1.36 s vs 0.57 s, Arcene 0.22 s vs 0.09 s). The milk documentation page (pythonhosted.org/milk/benchmarks.html, Intel Core2 6600 2.40GHz, versions not stated, times normalised to the fastest) shows the same direction for k-means: Shogun 2.02, scikits.learn 6.74, milk 1.0.

notes: Numbers and hardware match doc/index.rst exactly; repo metadata checked (BSD-3-Clause with optional GPL3 components, 3.1k stars, 1.0k forks, last commit 2023-12-19, so stale). Shortcomings to record: 2011-vintage versions, page flags Shogun as failing on k-means and Arcene inertia is blank, k-means settings not equalised, slower than scikit-learn on SVM and kNN in the same suite.

corrections.caveats: SNIPPET ONLY: arxiv.org, web3.arxiv.org, hgpu.org, openreview.net and ar5iv were unreachable, so the paper was not opened; the LeNet millisecond figures come from WebSearch results and must be re-read on the paper (a later search snippet attributing 25/46 ms Torch and 121/203 ms Caffe figures to the study looks like a mix-up with the AlexNet rows of soumith/convnet-benchmarks and should be ignored). In the reachable soumith/convnet-benchmarks README (6-core i7-5930K, Titan X) Torch-7 native GPU convolution (SpatialConvolutionMM, which lives in torch/cunn) is not faster than Caffe: AlexNet 342 ms vs 324 ms, Overfeat 878 vs 823, OxfordNet 1105 vs 1068, layer-wise 1265 vs 1231 ms; the fast rows there are cuDNN or fbfft kernels called through Torch bindings. The Theano paper (arXiv 1605.02688, via search snippet) reports Theano slightly faster than Torch on an LSTM benchmark. The README states 'Torch is not in active development'; the last commits (2025-03-31) are merged typo and build-fix pull requests.

The 250x to 1180x gains are algorithmic (approximate vs exact volume), not implausible codegen gains.

corrections.baseline: VINCI 1.0.5 (exact polytope volume; package birkhoff for the Birkhoff polytopes) and Cousins and Vempala's Matlab volume implementation (reference [13] in the text; the Table 7 caption labels it [12], their SODA 2014 Gaussian-volume paper)
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated (C++ about 2.5K lines on CGAL's d-dimensional kernel, CGAL LP solver with GMP, CGAL approximate minimum ellipsoid, Eigen, Boost mt19937)
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (SoCG 2014, Emiris and Fisikopoulos 'Efficient random-walk methods for approximating polytope volume'; volesti lists it in docs/misc/publications.md) but measures the 2014 precursor code (then on sourceforge randgeom), not today's volesti; PDF read from the author's GitHub pages repo; compiler and flags missing, so B and not A. Approximate versus exact answers are not the same task. Exact VINCI is faster on many low-dimensional inputs: cube-10 0.01 s vs 0.42 s, cube-15 0.40 s vs 1.44 s, simplices 0.01 to 0.02 s vs 0.56 to 919.01 s, rv-8-10 0.01 s vs 0.37 s, rv-10-12 0.01 s vs 1.00 s, cc-8-10 0.05 s vs 1.95 s, Fm-5 0.02 s vs 0.69 s. The Birkhoff exact times (B8 1920 s, B9 8 days, B10 6160 days) come from the birkhoff package's published computations (the paper equates B10 to a single 1 GHz processor running for almost 17 years), not from runs on the test machine. Against the Cousins-Vempala Matlab code (C++ vs Matlab, 10 runs) VolEsti is faster only for d < 80 per the paper: cube-80 582.19 s vs 531.46 s, cube-90 875.69 vs 701.54, cube-100 1285.08 vs 884.43, B9 499.56 vs 420.07, B10 1034.74 vs 691.97 are slower; that code ran with eps = 0.1 against eps = 1 for VolEsti, and VolEsti does about 100 times more hit-and-run steps while returning 4 to 100 times smaller error on cube-d for d > 70 and 5 to 80 times on Birkhoff polytopes. The repo README and docs carry no benchmark numbers.

notes: All quoted Table 1 and Table 7 numbers, the hardware and the abstract sentence are on the PDF. Corrections: the record's caveat 'cube-60 and above slower' is wrong (cube-60 222.10 s vs 229.33 s and cube-70 358.93 vs 427.82 are VolEsti wins; slower from cube-80), simplex max time is 919.01 s, the Matlab code is reference [13] in the text, and Birkhoff exact times are literature figures.
